patient_information: A 35-year-old woman from Malawi who is known to be HIV-positive and has been on antiretroviral treatment for the past 3 years. Her CD4 count is unknown.
chief_complaint: Referral for an ocular tumour in the left eye, with symptoms progressing over 8 months.
history_of_present_illness: Symptoms started 8 months prior with a whitish lesion growing on the conjunctiva of her left eye. Despite treatment with non-specified eye drops and later, herbal eye drops from a traditional healer, the lesion grew bigger and turned reddish. Over the months, the lesion continued to grow, she lost her eyesight in the affected eye, and the pain increased, leading her to seek further care.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Malawi, a country in sub-Saharan Africa. Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) is commonly seen in HIV-positive individuals in tropical regions. HIV infection, ultraviolet radiation, and human papilloma virus (HPV) are strongly associated with OSSN.
physical_exam: There is localized swelling of the left eyeball and orbit with incomplete lid closure. Visual acuity is 6/6 on the right, while the left eye has no light perception. Her left preauricular lymph nodes are swollen. The rest of her physical examination is unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: The patient is known to be HIV-positive. No other diagnostic tests, such as a biopsy for histopathological examination, were performed as the patient refused surgical intervention.
differential_diagnosis: The most likely diagnosis was considered to be advanced ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN). Other malignant lesions that can look similar include amelanotic melanomas, lymphomas, or adenocarcinomas. In its early stages, the lesion might be confused with benign conditions such as pterygium, an amelanotic naevus, or a lipoma.
management_and_clinical_course: The recommended management was analgesic treatment and an extended exenteration of the left eyeball and orbit. However, the patient refused surgical intervention and would only accept conservative treatment. Her left orbit was covered with antibiotics and bandaged. After her pain was sufficiently controlled, she was discharged with an offer to return at any time and was asked to report to her antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinic for control of her viral load.
final_diagnosis: The suspected diagnosis is advanced ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN). This diagnosis is based on the clinical presentation of a progressive ocular tumor leading to blindness and pain in an HIV-positive woman from a high-prevalence region. Although histopathological confirmation was not obtained because the patient refused surgery, the clinical picture is highly characteristic of this condition.
